segments.say: It's been a week in the new flat, and Ines has done it again. She came through the door with her shopping bags, and her hand went straight to the wrong side of the wall. Nothing there, of course. She laughed this time, out loud, alone in the hallway. She even looked at her own hand for a second, as if it might explain itself. It didn't. But it did leave her with a small, genuinely interesting thought. If I didn't choose that, then what exactly did?

It's a fair question, and a surprisingly slippery one. We use the word habit all the time. A habit of biting our nails, a habit of making tea, a good habit, a bad habit. But when psychologists try to say exactly what a habit is, they're a little more careful than we usually are. They want to separate a true habit from something that's merely a thing we do often. Those two can look identical from the outside, and yet work very differently on the inside.

Here's the key idea. Going for a run every morning because you've decided that running is good for you is one thing. Reaching for the light switch without any decision at all is quite another. The first is driven by a goal. The second is driven by a setting, and a memory of what happened there before. A habit, in this sense, isn't defined by how often we do something. It's defined by what sets it off, and by how little thought is involved.

Researchers often describe it like this. There's a familiar setting, and within it, some kind of cue. The cue might be a place, a time of day, a person, or a feeling. Then there's a response, the thing you do. And all of it is built up through repetition, with some small reward along the way. The setting, the cue and the response, joined together by doing it again and again, until the link is there, ready and waiting.

show.title: What a habit is made of

segments.say: One of the clearest summaries of all this was written by two psychologists, Wendy Wood and Dennis Rünger. They published it in 2016, in a journal called the Annual Review of Psychology. It's a review, which means they didn't run one new experiment. Instead, they gathered together what many years of studies had found, and described how habits are learned, how they're triggered, and how they relate to our goals. Much of what we'll talk about tonight leans on their careful picture.

show.where: A review in the Annual Review of Psychology, published 2016
show.what: Psychology of Habit: what decades of research tell us

segments.say: One thing that picture makes very clear is that habits are learned. They aren't something we're born with, and they aren't something we decide to have. As we repeat an action in a stable setting, our memory gradually builds a link between that setting and that response. The authors describe it as learning associations between a context and a response. And it tends to happen without us noticing, a little like a path forming across a lawn, one footstep at a time.

Wood and Rünger describe habits in a phrase worth remembering. They call them an efficient, default mode of response. Default, in the way a phone has default settings, the way things are arranged unless you deliberately change them. And efficient, because a habit gets the job done without much fuss. It's a reminder that habits aren't a glitch in how we work. They are, in a quiet way, how we work most of the time.

So we can picture two different ways of acting. In one, you have a goal, you think about it, and you choose what to do. In the other, you arrive somewhere familiar, and your mind simply carries out what it has done there before. Psychologists sometimes say the first is goal-directed, and the second is habitual. Most days are a blend of the two, with the habitual one doing a lot more of the quiet work than we'd guess.

Put side by side, the differences are easy to see. A goal-directed action is chosen for what it will bring. A habit is set off by the situation you're standing in. A goal-directed action needs some attention, some thought. A habit needs very little. And one more difference, which matters a great deal tonight. A goal can change in an instant, the moment you change your mind. A habit has no mind to change. It just keeps following the cue.

show.title: Two ways of acting
items: Goal: chosen for what it brings
Habit: set off by the situation

segments.say: Which brings us back to the hallway, and to Ines's hand. This is the heart of what a habit is. A habit isn't chosen in the moment. It's triggered. Ines walks through her front door, and the door itself is the cue. The cue wakes the response, and the response runs, quite smoothly, before any decision has had a chance to form. By the time she notices, the hand has already arrived. It's rather like a tune you didn't mean to start humming.

The light switch is such a good example because Ines doesn't want to flip a switch that isn't there. Her goals haven't changed at all. She simply wants light. But the old setting, the old door, the old sequence of steps, were repeated so many times that her hand learned them well. And her hand doesn't know she moved. It's carrying out its lesson faithfully, in a place where the lesson no longer applies. That's both a little funny and a little tender.

show.sub: Why the switch is so useful

segments.say: Here is a result from that review that tends to surprise people. When an action has been repeated many times in the same setting, what people say they intend to do predicts their behavior less well. For rarely repeated actions, intentions do a decent job. But for well-worn routines, the setting itself starts to do more of the steering. In other words, for a strong habit, what we mean to do and what we actually do can quietly drift apart.

show.what: When an action is repeated often, intentions predict it less well

segments.say: Why would a mind work this way? Wood and Rünger point to something simple. Deliberate thinking uses working memory, and working memory is limited. We can only hold and weigh so much at once. Habits bypass that limit. They let an action run without needing much of that precious attention. So when we're busy, distracted, or hurried, the habit is still there, working away, while our thoughts are somewhere else entirely.

It's a useful trade, really. A habit saves us time, because we don't have to work out what to do. It saves attention, so we can think about other things. It saves us a thousand tiny decisions, like which pocket the keys go in. And it saves a little energy, since a familiar action tends to feel easier than a brand-new one. Seen like this, a habit is a kind of gift our past self leaves for our future self.

Still, there's a catch, and it's the same catch James noticed. The cue doesn't check whether the response is still wanted. Take Ines and her phone. In her old flat, lying down in bed became a cue, very gradually, for picking up her phone. Now she's in a new bed, in a new city, but she still lies down in the same way. And her hand reaches, in the same way, as if nothing at all had changed.

That's what Ines notices, lying there a little later that evening. She doesn't feel a strong urge. She doesn't even feel tempted. It's simply that the phone is in her hand, and the screen is glowing. My hand knew before I did, she thinks. And that, in a single sentence, is a rather good description of a habit. A response that arrives ahead of the decision, called forward by a cue we hardly noticed.

show.text: My hand knew before I did.

segments.say: So perhaps we can set one idea down for good. The idea that a habit means a weak will, or a lazy character. A habit is a learned link between a setting and an action, built by repetition, kept because it was useful once. It isn't a moral failing. It's closer to a well-worn path through a field. And once you can see the path clearly, you can begin to ask, kindly, where you'd like a new one to go.

show.cap: A gentler way to see it

segments.say: In a little while, we'll look at what's happening in the brain when a habit takes over, and why it can seem to carry on even when we no longer want what it brings. But for now, let's let Ines settle. Her hand has found the lamp at last, on the right-hand side, somewhere around the fourth try. The flat is quiet. Outside, a bus goes by, then nothing. Take a slow breath, and let this idea rest, for a moment, like a stone in warm water.
